title: [B1 • Band 5.0] Bài 107: The Kauri Forests of New Zealand
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 107 (LEVEL B1 • BAND 5.0)

The Kauri Forests of New Zealand

Paragraph 1. Growing high above the forests of northern New Zealand, the kauri tree is one of the largest and longest-living trees on the planet. Mature kauri trees can reach over fifty metres in height, with thick trunks over five metres wide, and individual trees have survived for more than two millennia. For the native Māori people, the giant kauri was a sacred spiritual symbol known as Tāne Mahuta, or Lord of the Forest. Māori builders respected living trees and collected only fallen logs to carve giant ocean-going war canoes, while also using tree bark to make dark tattoo pigments.

Paragraph 2. The arrival of European settlers in the late eighteenth century changed the future of these forests completely. British naval ships quickly noticed that tall, straight, knot-free kauri trunks were ideal for building strong ship masts and wooden poles. Throughout the nineteenth century, a massive timber industry grew across northern New Zealand. Because the enormous logs were far too heavy for bullock teams on steep mountain trails, logging companies constructed huge wooden dams across narrow river valleys. Once rainwater filled the space behind a dam, workers blasted the gates open, sending a powerful flood that carried hundreds of logs downstream to coastal mills.

Paragraph 3. Alongside timber logging, a huge business developed around kauri gum between the 1870s and 1920s. This hardened ancient resin had leaked from damaged trees over thousands of years and collected inside underground swamps. Thousands of European and Dalmatian immigrants worked as gum-diggers, probing soft wetlands with steel spears and digging up fossilised lumps weighing up to twenty kilograms. Kauri gum soon became a major New Zealand export, providing a vital ingredient for high-quality varnishes, outdoor paints, and linoleum flooring across Europe and North America.

Paragraph 4. By the mid-twentieth century, uncontrolled tree cutting and gum digging had wiped out over ninety-five percent of the original kauri forests. Just as new laws began protecting the remaining trees, a deadly new threat appeared in the early 2000s. Scientists noticed mature trees developing yellow leaves, dying upper branches, and leaking sticky liquid around their lower trunks. Researchers identified the cause as kauri dieback disease, driven by an aggressive soil-living organism.

Paragraph 5. This disease is currently incurable and destroys the internal tubes that carry water and nutrients up the tree, slowly starving it to death. Because the tiny spores travel almost entirely inside wet soil particles, walkers along popular forest tracks have become the main way the infection spreads. To protect healthy forests, environmental agencies have placed mandatory cleaning stations at trail entrances, requiring visitors to scrub every trace of mud from their footwear and spray disinfectant.
